messages.tour.1.title: 1. Choose a shape
messages.tour.1.text: Make a NACA wing or a built-in body, or upload your own part from SolidWorks (STEP or STL). WindLab checks that the surface is closed and shows it in 3D: the wind blows along x, z is up.
messages.tour.2.title: 2. Check the units and the size
messages.tour.2.text: A STEP file says which units it uses; an STL file does not, so you choose them. Either way, read the size WindLab reports ("Your part is 30 cm long") before you run: a part that would be 300 m long is a units mistake. The Turn 90° buttons face the part into the wind.
messages.tour.3.title: 3. Set the conditions
messages.tour.3.text: Airspeed (1-100 m/s) and the angle of attack, or an angle sweep of up to 8 angles on one mesh. The Reynolds number updates as you type; Quick is the everyday mesh and the page tells you how long a run should take on this computer.
messages.tour.4.title: 4. Preview the airflow (instant)
messages.tour.4.text: A 2D sketch of the flow, drawn in your browser while you change the angle. It is not the full simulation, but it shows where the air speeds up, slows down and separates.
messages.tour.5.title: 5. Run the wind tunnel
messages.tour.5.text: The real simulation: one to a few minutes. You can watch the lift and drag coefficients settle, see which stage is running, and stop the run at any time.
messages.tour.6.title: 6. Results, reports, comparisons and lessons
messages.tour.6.text: Lift, drag and L/D with the range where the true value most likely lies, the pressure on the part in 3D, the flow through the middle, and downloads: a printable report, CSV files and the OpenFOAM case. Under My runs you can compare 2 to 5 runs; the Lessons walk you through five classic experiments. Every number is from an uncalibrated prototype: learn and compare, do not design real hardware with it.

messages.page.hStart: New here? Start with a lesson
messages.page.startCard.p: WindLab puts a part in a virtual wind tunnel and shows its lift and drag. The quickest way in is the first guided lesson, Lift vs angle of attack (about 50 minutes; it comes with pre-computed results, so nothing has to be calculated to start). Or take the two-minute tour of the page, or simply press Make this wing below and then Run the wind tunnel.
messages.page.tour.span: Esc closes the tour; you can reopen it any time with "Take the tour" at the top.
messages.page.about.p: SenSym WindLab is a virtual wind tunnel for engineering students: it meshes a part, runs the open-source OpenFOAM® solver on your own computer and shows the lift and drag. Uncalibrated prototype — not yet validated. For educational and preliminary design use; not for airworthiness or safety determinations.

messages.page.def.laminarAndTurbulent: What do laminar and turbulent mean?
messages.page.results.summary.2: What do these numbers mean, and how much can I trust them?
messages.page.results.p.9: C<sub>L</sub> and C<sub>D</sub> are the lift and drag forces divided by the dynamic pressure of the wind (½ρV²) and the reference area, so they do not depend on the size of the part or the speed, only on its shape, its angle to the wind and the Reynolds number. L/D is simply their ratio. The pitching moment C<sub>m</sub> (under More details) is taken about the reference point, the quarter-chord for the built-in wings. The "wobble" is how much C<sub>L</sub> and C<sub>D</sub> still moved over the last solver iterations: it tells you whether the calculation settled, not whether it is right.
messages.page.results.p.10: Accuracy. The flow solver itself was checked in 2D against NASA's NACA 0012 reference at Re 6 million: lift within 2 % and drag within 1 % of the reference. The Quick mesh you are using is much coarser. On the built-in NACA 0012 wing it gives lift within a few percent of what a finer mesh gives, but drag about 9 % too high (8 % at 10°) compared with what the same method gives on a mesh ten times finer, and about a third above the validated 2D calculation at the same Reynolds number, because the surface cells are coarse (see the mesh study in the project's validation folder). On top of that, WindLab assumes the boundary layer is turbulent from the leading edge; at the Reynolds numbers of a student-size model (10⁵ to 10⁶) real air keeps a laminar run first, so measured drag is lower again, often by a third. Treat CD as an upper estimate and L/D as a lower one, and compare runs made on the same mesh with each other: trends and differences are far more trustworthy than absolute drag. A part that is symmetric top to bottom has zero lift at 0°; a small CL shown there is numerical noise from the mesh, not physics. Thin fins or plates thinner than a mesh cell would make it large, so WindLab measures the thickness of every uploaded part and refines the mesh around such parts on its own (the "Thin parts" note under the mesh choice says when).

messages.page.lessons.p: Five guided lessons of about 50 minutes each. Every lesson asks you to predict before you run, then observe and explain, and ends with three quick questions. You can run the cases yourself (a few minutes each) or use the pre-computed results that ship with WindLab. Your answers are saved on this computer only and go into windlab feedback export.

messages.lesson.run.help.noPack: "Set up this run for me" fills in Steps 1 and 2; you then press "Run the wind tunnel" in Step 3. No pre-computed result is installed for this step.
messages.lesson.note.settingUp: Setting up the shape and the conditions…
messages.lesson.note.filled: Steps 1 and 2 are filled in. Press "Run the wind tunnel" in Step 3, then come back to this lesson.
messages.lesson.note.loaded: The pre-computed results are open in Step 4 and listed under My runs. Come back here for the next step.
messages.lesson.note.allLoaded: All {n} pre-computed results are listed (and ticked) under My runs{compared}; this step's run is open in Step 4. Come back here for the next step.
messages.lesson.note.allCompared: and shown side by side under Compare runs
messages.lesson.wrong: ✗ Not quite. The right answer is: {answer}
messages.demo.uploadOff: — install WindLab to upload your own part (STEP or STL)
messages.preview.note.restart: The preview starts again from still air.
messages.preview.note.contextLost: The graphics card stopped drawing the preview (it may be busy). Press Play to start it again.
messages.preview.note.reducedMotion: The animation is paused because your system asks for less motion. Press Play to run it, or "Advance 200 steps" to move the flow on without animation.
messages.preview.note.unstable: The preview started again: the flow became unstable (this can happen at large angles or with very sharp edges).
messages.preview.re: Preview Reynolds number ≈ {re} — {own}. A lower Reynolds number means stickier air: thicker boundary layers and earlier separation than in the full simulation.
messages.preview.readout.waiting: Lattice steps so far: {steps}. The forces appear after a moment.
messages.preview.readout: Rough 2D estimate from the preview{settling}: lift coefficient ≈ {cl}, drag coefficient ≈ {cd}, lift ÷ drag ≈ {ld} ({steps} lattice steps, {mode}).
messages.preview.text: {what} The wind blows from left to right; the dark outlined shape is the cut through the middle of {name}, turned by the angle of attack ({alpha}°).
messages.preview.text.speed: Colours show the air speed: dark purple = slow or stopped air (in front of the part and in its wake), green = about the wind speed, yellow = faster than the wind (over the top of a wing at a positive angle).
messages.preview.text.swirl: Colours show the swirl (vorticity): red = turning anticlockwise, blue = clockwise, white = no swirl. The two sheets shed from the part's edges are its boundary layers leaving as a wake.
messages.preview.viewLabel: Animated airflow sketch around the mid-span outline of {name} at {alpha} degrees, coloured by {field}. The numbers below give a rough lift and drag estimate.
messages.viewer.wheelHint: Ctrl + scroll to zoom (or click the view first)
messages.chart.liveLabel: {name} against solver iteration; latest {value} at iteration {iteration}
